This is a long touted myth. Most people with the "STEM" degrees don't go into STEM fields, and most of them end up in jobs that don't require a degree. And that doesn't even take into account all of the students who drop out before graduating because they realize they won't get jobs.

Point in case, the university I attended (which was the feeder school to all the major industry in the metropolitan area, including companies like Siemens, Boeing, and Lockheed) had a <10% rate of student internships and post-graduation employment. Those that could afford to go to grad school did, some completed their degrees, and ~25% of their students dropped out by Junior or Senior year because they couldn't afford to go on without hope of employment following graduation. These were numbers I got directly from the heads of the science and engineer departments (whom I spoke with when trying to decide whether to continue with my own degree).

You could, of course, make the argument that even if you don't get an engineering job, having an engineering degree looks good on a resume. And sometimes it does. But many employers get scared because they think you'll jump ship the second you get a job opportunity in an engineering field and won't want to hire you. It ends up being a push, and you probably would have been just as well off with a history or liberal arts degree.

The social connections you make in college are far more important than your major. You know what helps with that? Having wealthy, well-connected parents.

That might be true, but it was my experience and the experience of ever single one of my peers and most of them graduated just after the crash. I never graduated because I gave up after sending out literally hundreds of employment applications, signing up with 3 different internship placement firms, and visiting every local business in my areas as well as a few personal contacts and not encountering any jobs prospects, and being discouraged by the dismal picture I encountered when talking to the heads at my local university (I was a math and computer science major with a >3.8 GPA but I would have been willing to switch to literally any technical major if I had better prospects). 3 of my friends graduated as engineers with >3.5 GPAs, none of them could find work, all joined the military. Another one was a math and comp sci major who applied to grad school after not being able to find work, and eventually got a job at Google after drawing his masters out for 3 years.

But experience is irrelevant, statistics are truth. The truth is that the majority of STEM majors don't end up in STEM fields, and among those who don't end up in STEM fields the majority of those end up in jobs that don't require a degree, making an engineering or science degree only marginally more useful than any other degree in underwater basket-weaving.

Edit: I also have worked as a hiring manager in a civil construction and engineering company and would get dozens of applications every week from engineering graduates who were desperate, couldn't find work, and were willing to take any grunt-level position if it meant the were getting paid.
